What a Travel Advisor Actually Does (And Why It's Worth It)

The honest answer is less glamorous than the brochure version. Most of what we do is logistics, relationships, and knowing which questions to ask before you've thought to ask them.

Home / Travel Journal / Planning Advice / What a Travel Advisor Actually Does
MS
Mark Sole Founder & Travel Director, Hit Your Mark Travel
Share

People ask me what I do, and I tell them I'm a travel advisor. The follow-up is almost always some version of the same question: "Can't you just book everything online yourself now?" The honest answer is yes, you can. You can also do your own taxes, represent yourself in a legal dispute, and cut your own hair. The question isn't whether you're capable. It's whether the outcome is the same.

The travel industry spent fifteen years telling people that advisors were obsolete — that booking engines made us unnecessary. What those fifteen years actually produced was a generation of travelers who know how to find a hotel on a website but have no idea what they're missing when they do. I'm going to try to explain what that is.

"The value isn't in the booking. The booking is the easy part. The value is in everything that happened before you were even thinking about a booking."

What we actually do all day

On any given Tuesday, I might spend the morning on the phone with a camp manager in Botswana confirming whether the vehicle policy has changed for the upcoming dry season. I'll spend part of the afternoon reviewing a client's revised itinerary after an airline routing changed. I'll respond to an email from someone in the middle of their honeymoon who needs a dinner reservation moved because their flight was delayed by three hours. And at some point, I'll sit down with a new client to figure out where they actually want to go — which is a different conversation than where they think they want to go.

None of that is glamorous. There's no single moment where expertise becomes dramatic. It's incremental — a hundred small decisions made correctly, most of which the client never sees. The measure of a good advisor isn't what happens when things go smoothly. It's what happens when they don't, and whether you were already in position to handle it.

The relationship problem that booking engines can't solve

The most significant thing a good travel advisor brings to a trip isn't information. You can find information. What you can't replicate is a decade of maintained professional relationships with the right people at the right properties — and the resulting access those relationships produce.

Here's what that looks like in practice. When I book a client into a resort I've worked with for years, the general manager knows my clients are likely to be low-maintenance, appreciative, and good guests. That reputation, built over time, translates into real things: room upgrades that aren't available to book online, priority reservations at restaurants that show as full on every platform, small additions — a bottle of wine at arrival, a note, early check-in — that don't show up in any rate comparison tool. These aren't guaranteed on every trip, but they happen consistently because the relationship is real.

When you book direct or through a general booking site, you're one transaction among thousands. When I book on your behalf, I'm a known quantity with a track record. Those are different positions to be in.

Behind the Scenes · Travel Planning

The work that determines how a trip feels is mostly invisible — done weeks or months before the client arrives anywhere.

The questions you don't know to ask

This is where I think advisors add the most value that's hardest to see. Most travelers know what they want. What they don't know is what they haven't thought to consider — and the gap between those two things can be the difference between a trip that was fine and one that was exceptional.

A client comes to me wanting a safari. They've decided on Kenya because they've seen the Masai Mara on a nature documentary. They want to go in August. Those are reasonable starting points. But here are the questions they haven't asked yet:

  • How many vehicles does the camp allow at a sighting? The answer ranges from two to unlimited, and that difference will define every game drive they take.
  • What's the guide's background — wildlife biology, tracking, years in the specific reserve? A guide who has spent twenty years in one ecosystem sees things a generalist misses.
  • Is the camp inside or outside the reserve boundary? The distinction affects vehicle access, night drives, and off-road capability in ways that matter enormously in practice.
  • What does the camp's wet-season access look like? If a second airport is involved, and one of those legs is on a six-seat Cessna, they should know that before they book.
  • Are they open to adding northern Tanzania to the itinerary? In August, the wildebeest migration is actually split across the Serengeti and the Mara — a combined itinerary might give them more of what they actually came for.

None of these questions would have occurred to them before the trip. Several of them would have occurred to them during the trip, at which point it's too late to change anything.

"Most travelers know what they want. What they don't know is what they haven't thought to consider — and the gap between those two things is where the trip is won or lost."

The financial case (which is more straightforward than people expect)

The assumption most people make is that using an advisor costs more. In many cases, the opposite is true. Travel advisors who are part of preferred partner networks — Virtuoso, Signature, and similar consortia — have access to rates and amenities that are not available to the public. At certain properties, particularly in the luxury segment, booking through an advisor is genuinely the best available rate, plus added value.

Where advisors do charge fees, those fees are typically structured around planning and consultation — not the individual booking. A flat planning fee for a two-week safari is a small fraction of the total trip cost, and the value it produces — in avoided mistakes, better allocation of budget, and access to experiences that can't be booked any other way — generally exceeds that cost by a wide margin.

The more useful frame isn't "does the advisor cost money?" It's "what does a mistake cost?" Getting the camp selection wrong on a safari, spending your honeymoon in a room that wasn't what you expected, or losing three days of a ten-day trip to a routing problem you didn't anticipate — those have real costs. Getting them right has a value that doesn't show up in a booking comparison.

A note on fees

Hit Your Mark Travel charges a planning fee for itinerary design and consultation. That fee covers the research, the calls, the contingency planning, and the ongoing support from the moment you reach out to the moment you return. It does not cover the trip itself — hotels, flights, and ground arrangements are quoted and booked separately. If you're comparing advisors, ask specifically what the fee covers and what it doesn't. The answer tells you a lot about how they work.

What to look for in an advisor — and what to avoid

Not all advisors are the same. Some are generalists who will book you into whatever property is generating the highest commission that month. Some specialize in specific destinations or travel types and know those areas with real depth. The distinction matters, and it's worth asking about directly.

A few things worth asking any advisor before you work with them:

  • Have you been there? Not "have you read about it" — have you personally visited the property, the destination, the camp? First-hand experience is not optional. It's the whole point.
  • How do you get paid? Commission, fee, or both. The answer is less important than the honesty of it. An advisor who's evasive about their compensation structure is telling you something.
  • What happens if something goes wrong mid-trip? Who do you call? What's the response time? This is when the relationship matters most, and it's worth knowing in advance.
  • Can you show me a sample itinerary for a trip like mine? Not a brochure — an actual itinerary, the kind of document you'd receive if you booked. The quality of that document reflects the quality of the planning behind it.

The honest version of the pitch

I don't think everyone needs a travel advisor for every trip. If you're booking a weekend in a city you know well, or a direct flight and one hotel, you don't need me. The tools exist, you know what you want, and the margin for error is low.

Where it becomes worth it is when the complexity increases, the stakes are higher, or the destination is unfamiliar enough that your assumptions about it might be wrong. A safari, a honeymoon, a multi-country itinerary, a trip involving places that require real local knowledge — these are the situations where the cost of getting it wrong is meaningful and the value of getting it right is significant.

The best trips I've ever planned didn't feel like they involved an advisor at all. The client arrived, everything worked, and they had an experience that exceeded what they thought they were booking. That's the goal. The invisible work beforehand is what makes the visible experience possible.
